question:
For Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 119 (OMIM #621304), caused by variants in RNU2-2: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Reported clinical phenotypes in affected individuals with exact numerator and denominator per cohort (not percentage alone), verbatim paper description, and matching HPO term if identifiable
Source attribution (PMID or DOI) and cohort specification for every reported phenotype frequency
Most discriminating findings present in most affected individuals but uncommon in differential/overlapping disorders, naming the disorders and rating confidence of the distinction
Findings looked for and found absent in affected individuals that argue against the diagnosis if present
Phenotype differences/correlations by variant type, variant position, age, or sex
Findings reported in one paper and explicitly contradicted by another

DEE119.definition: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 119 (DEE119; OMIM #621304) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the small nuclear RNA (snRNA) gene RNU2-2, characterized clinically by neurodevelopmental delay, severe intellectual disability, and frequent epilepsy.

source.title: Systematic analysis of snRNA genes reveals frequent RNU2-2 variants in dominant and recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
source.quote: phenotype associated with dominant or biallelic RNU2-2 variants is characterized by neurodevelopmental delay, severe ID and epilepsy

OMIM #621304.definition: OMIM #621304 designates Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy 119 (DEE119), a severe neurodevelopmental disorder and spliceosomopathy caused by pathogenic variants in the non-coding small nuclear RNA gene RNU2-2. It is characterized by global developmental delay, severe-to-profound intellectual disability, refractory seizures, and hyperkinetic movement disorders.

RNU2-2.definition: A non-coding small nuclear RNA (snRNA) gene that forms an essential component of the spliceosome; pathogenic variants in RNU2-2 cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) and neurodevelopmental disorders manifesting with refractory seizures and profound intellectual and developmental impairment.

source.title: Pathogenic Variants in RNU2‐2, a Non‐coding Spliceosomal RNA, Cause a Distinctive Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy
source.quote: RNU2-2 is a non-coding small nuclear RNA (snRNA) that forms part of the spliceosome.

U2 small nuclear RNA (snRNA).definition: A non-coding small nuclear RNA molecule that is incorporated into the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U2 snRNP) complex as an essential component of the major spliceosome, where it mediates pre-mRNA splicing by recognizing the intronic branch site via base pairing. Pathogenic variants in genes encoding U2 snRNA, such as RNU2-2, disrupt splicing and cause severe neurodevelopmental disorders, specifically developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.

source.quote: RNU2- 2 encodes a U2 snRNA variant that is incorporated into the major spliceosome as part of the U2 snRNP and represents a central component of the major spliceosome.

prior.text: DEE119 cannot be reliably distinguished from other monogenic early-onset DEEs (e.g., STXBP1, SCN1A, KCNQ2, or RNU4-2-related DEE) by clinical phenotype alone, as the hallmark features (infantile-onset refractory epilepsy, severe developmental regression/arrest, axial hypotonia, and microcephaly) overlap broadly across epileptic encephalopathies. However, a pattern of early infantile epileptic spasms or tonic seizures paired with severe secondary microcephaly, stereotypic hand movements, and lack of structural brain malformations on MRI increases clinical suspicion in whole-genome negative DEE cases.
candidate_answers: Global developmental delay / intellectual disability (HP:0001263) and intractable early-onset seizures (HP:0001250) are present in virtually all (>90-95%) documented individuals with RNU2-2-associated DEE119.
Progressive or postnatal microcephaly (HP:0005484) and severe axial hypotonia (HP:0008936) are present in over 60-80% of affected patients.

No single clinical finding uniquely discriminates DEE119 from other severe non-coding or coding DEEs (such as RNU4-2-related neurodevelopmental disorder, CDKL5 deficiency, or STXBP1 encephalopathy); diagnosis requires molecular genetic confirmation via whole-genome sequencing.
Normal developmental milestones prior to seizure onset or completely normal baseline EEG in infancy are expected to be absent in affected individuals; their presence strongly argues against DEE119.

Variants cluster at specific, invariant functional bases (e.g., branchpoint recognition or spliceosomal catalytic core interaction domains of the snRNA), with recurrent de novo single nucleotide changes exhibiting highly congruent, severe phenotypes across sexes.

d1.question_text: What are the precise published cohort sizes (numerators and denominators) and exact HPO frequencies in the primary discovery papers defining DEE119 (OMIM #621304)?
d1.alloc_rationale: Directly resolves requirement 1 by extracting exact numerators, denominators, verbatim clinical descriptions, and matching HPO terms with PMIDs from discovery cohorts.

d2.question_text: Does RNU2-2-related encephalopathy have distinguishing dysmorphic, ocular, or skeletal features compared to RNU4-2-associated neurodevelopmental disorder?

d3.question_text: Are there recurrent hotspot positions in RNU2-2 (analogous to the 18-bp structural element hotspots seen in RNU4-2), and do specific variants correlate with milder or non-epileptic presentations?

d4.question_text: What specific EEG patterns (e.g., hypsarrhythmia, burst-suppression, multifocal epileptiform discharges) predominate in the reported cohorts?

d5.question_text: Have any contradictory clinical findings been described between initial case series regarding structural neuroimaging abnormalities (e.g., cerebral atrophy or delayed myelination vs. normal initial MRI)?

d6.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Global developmental delay / intellectual disability (HP:0001263) and intractable early-onset seizures (HP:0001250) are present in virtually all (>90-95%) documented individuals with RNU2-2-associated DEE119.
d6.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Epilepsy penetrance: While global developmental delay/ID is observed in >95% of individuals older than 3 years, Leitão et al. report 16 of 141 individuals lacking epilepsy (~85% penetrance), directly refuting the hypothesis that seizures are present in >90-95% of all RNU2-2-associated disease cases.; Age of seizure onset: The hypothesis posits early-onset seizures, but Chiu et al. reported a median seizure onset age of 24 months, indicating childhood rather than early infantile onset in substantial portions of the cohort.

d7.question_text: Does epilepsy penetrance and age of onset differ significantly between dominant de novo RNU2-2 variants and recessive biallelic RNU2-2 variants?
d7.rationale: Leitão et al. and Jackson et al. describe both dominant and recessive RNU2-2-associated disorders, but dominant versus recessive sub-cohort seizure rates and phenotypes need stratification to evaluate whether DEE119 strict definition accounts for non-epileptic neurodevelopmental phenotypes.
d7.alloc_rationale: Disentangles dominant DEE119 from recessive RNU2-2 cohorts to resolve conflicts regarding seizure penetrance, age of onset, and variant-specific phenotypic distinctions.

d8.question_text: What is the discriminatory diagnostic power of combining hyperkinesia/movement disorders and sleep apnea/hyperventilation with intellectual disability to distinguish RNU2-2 DEE from other noncoding spliceosomopathies such as RNU4-2?
d8.rationale: Both Henry et al. and Chiu et al. note distinctive features (hyperkinesia, hyperventilation, sleep apnea, hippocampal sclerosis) which could allow clinicians to phenotype RNU2-2 patients apart from RNU4-2 ReNU syndrome.
d8.alloc_rationale: Directly targets the phenotypic discrimination criteria separating RNU2-2 DEE from its primary differential diagnostic lookalike, RNU4-2 ReNU syndrome.

d9.question_text: Does the specific combination of early hyperkinesia/chorea, episodic central hyperventilation, and early hippocampal sclerosis provide a high positive predictive value for RNU2-2 variants when evaluated across large unsolved DEE registries?
d9.rationale: While individual features overlap with other DEEs (e.g., Rett syndrome hyperventilation, STXBP1 movement disorders), multivariate scoring of this feature triad could prioritize RNU2-2 targeted testing in low-resource settings.

d10.question_text: Can functional transcriptomic biomarkers, such as the U2-2 to U2-1 abundance ratio or tissue-specific alternate 3' splice site usage in fibroblasts, serve as conclusive non-genomic diagnostic assays for DEE119?
d10.rationale: Jackson et al. and Henry et al. identify U2-2:U2-1 ratio depletion and aberrant fibroblast splicing patterns, which could resolve variants of uncertain significance in non-coding snRNA genes.

d11.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Variants cluster at specific, invariant functional bases (e.g., branchpoint recognition or spliceosomal catalytic core interaction domains of the snRNA), with recurrent de novo single nucleotide changes exhibiting highly congruent, severe phenotypes across sexes.
d11.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Dominant de novo variants do not exclusively cause a uniform, severe DEE; phenotypes span a continuum down to mild learning disability without epilepsy (4/16 non-epileptic patients carried dominant pathogenic variants in Leitão et al.).; The disease architecture is not dominated exclusively by recurrent de novo mutations; recessive biallelic RNU2-2 alterations occur at more than double the frequency of dominant variants in large cohorts (91 biallelic vs 35 dominant cases in Leitão et al.) and represent a distinct molecular mechanism involving reduced U2-2 stability.

d12.question_text: What specific nucleotide-level or structural features distinguish RNU2-2 variants that manifest as dominant DEE from those that cause mild intellectual disability without epilepsy or require biallelic transmission?
d12.rationale: Large cohort studies demonstrate a gradient of clinical severity across dominant and recessive forms, suggesting subtle positional or functional determinants govern phenotypic penetration.

d13.question_text: Can tissue-specific mis-splicing profiles in accessible patient cells reliably differentiate RNU2-2 encephalopathy from phenocopying spliceosomopathies such as ReNU syndrome (RNU4-2)?
d13.rationale: Fibroblast RNA sequencing reveals distinct alternative 3' splice site usage and mutually exclusive exon events in RNU2-2, but these signatures are suppressed or absent in blood cells.

d14.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Progressive or postnatal microcephaly (HP:0005484) and severe axial hypotonia (HP:0008936) are present in over 60-80% of affected patients.
d14.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: OMIM #621304 is classified as autosomal dominant developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 119, whereas the quantitative 79% hypotonia frequency is specifically derived from individuals with biallelic (recessive) RNU2-2 variants.; Jackson et al. (2026) state that recessive RNU2-2 syndrome is clinically distinct from the dominant disorder, preventing direct extrapolation of phenotypic frequencies between dominant DEE 119 and recessive RNU2-2 cohorts.; While microcephaly is frequently noted as a comorbid feature, existing published cohorts do not confirm that progressive or postnatal microcephaly independently achieves the hypothesized 60-80% frequency threshold.

d15.question_text: What is the exact penetrance of postnatal versus congenital microcephaly in dominant versus biallelic RNU2-2 cohorts?
d15.rationale: Differentiating head circumference trajectories between dominant DEE 119 and recessive RNU2-2 encephalopathies is critical to establishing whether microcephaly serves as a reliable discriminating biomarker.

d16.question_text: How do co-occurring axial hypotonia and appendicular hypertonia differentiate RNU2-2 DEE from other noncoding spliceosomal encephalopathies (such as RNU4-2-related ReNU syndrome)?
d16.rationale: Henry et al. observed co-occurring hypotonia (79%) and hypertonia (79%) in biallelic RNU2-2 patients, a mixed motor phenotype that could improve phenotypic specificity relative to clinically overlapping DEEs.

d17.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Normal developmental milestones prior to seizure onset or completely normal baseline EEG in infancy are expected to be absent in affected individuals; their presence strongly argues against DEE119.
d17.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Krygier et al. (2026) report that DEE119 features developmental regression, indicating that some milestones can be achieved before loss, which contradicts the hypothesis that normal pre-seizure milestones are strictly absent.; Chiu et al. (2026) demonstrate that median seizure onset occurs relatively late in infancy/early childhood (24 months), yet baseline EEGs in early infancy prior to seizure onset have not been systematically established as universally abnormal across all patients.

d18.question_text: What is the precise trajectory of motor and language milestone acquisition prior to the reported regression and seizure onset in dominant versus recessive RNU2-2 cohorts?
d18.rationale: Clarifying whether regression occurs from a normal developmental baseline or on top of preexisting global developmental delay will resolve whether normal early milestones can truly rule out DEE119.

d19.question_text: What are the earliest detectable prospective electroencephalographic abnormalities in asymptomatic or pre-seizure infants carrying pathogenic RNU2-2 variants?
d19.rationale: Determining whether sleep-activated multifocal discharges precede seizure onset or are completely absent in early infancy will establish the negative predictive value of a normal baseline infant EEG.

d20.question_text: Build on the confirmed prior: No single clinical finding uniquely discriminates DEE119 from other severe non-coding or coding DEEs (such as RNU4-2-related neurodevelopmental disorder, CDKL5 deficiency, or STXBP1 encephalopathy); diagnosis requires molecular genetic confirmation via whole-genome sequencing.

d21.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for hyperventilation episodes, microcephaly, and seizure types specifically within the 35 dominant DEE119 patients reported by Leitão et al. (2026)?
d21.rationale: Extracting the full supplementary clinical table from Leitão et al. will provide standard HPO terms and exact frequencies for the dominant DEE119 subcohort.
d21.alloc_rationale: Directly resolves required clinical phenotype frequencies, verbatim descriptions, and HPO mappings with exact numerators and denominators from the dominant DEE119 cohort in Leitao et al.

d22.question_text: Does the phenotypic spectrum of dominant RNU2-2 DEE119 differ significantly from the recessive biallelic RNU2-2 cohort (n=91) in seizure onset age, severity of intellectual disability, or structural brain anomalies?
d22.rationale: Determining whether dominant and recessive forms display distinctive clinical hallmarks will prevent misattribution of recessive features to dominant DEE119.

d23.question_text: Does the specific combination of compound heterozygous variants (e.g., promoter/loss-of-expression allele in trans with 5' core coding variant) modulate seizure onset and refractoriness in recessive RNU2-2 syndrome?
d23.rationale: Leitão et al. and Greene et al. found that recessive cases frequently harbor de novo mutations in trans with inherited alleles across varying domains of RNU2-2. Dissecting allelic series will test whether residual U2-2 expression correlates with the presence or absence of epilepsy.

d24.question_text: What is the detailed comparative seizure semiology and drug responsiveness between dominant de novo and biallelic RNU2-2 cohorts?
d24.rationale: Henry et al. observed high rates of infantile spasms, tonic seizures, and Lennox-Gastaut patterns in biallelic patients. Evaluating whether dominant cases share these specific semiologies or respond differently to anti-seizure medications will clarify whether DEE119 clinical classification requires inheritance-stratified sub-phenotyping.

d25.question_text: What specific neurological signs (e.g. movement disorder sub-phenotypes or seizure semiology) reliably distinguish dominant de novo RNU2-2 encephalopathy from biallelic recessive RNU2-2 encephalopathy?
d25.rationale: While both modes of inheritance share severe developmental delay and high epilepsy rates (>80%), Krygier et al. noted hyperkinetic movement disorders are significantly enriched in biallelic cases, warranting systematic head-to-head clinical phenotyping.

d26.question_text: Can the ratio of U2-2 to its paralog U2-1 serve as a sensitive clinical biomarker to discriminate between monoallelic dominant and biallelic recessive RNU2-2 cases?
d26.rationale: Jackson et al. and Greene et al. observed marked reduction (>90%) of pathogenic U2-2 transcripts in biallelic individuals with wild-type compensation in monoallelic carriers, suggesting transcript dosage ratios could offer diagnostic resolution.

d27.question_text: What is the exact sensitivity and positive predictive value of episodic central hyperventilation when discriminating dominant DEE119 from ReNU syndrome (RNU4-2) and Rett-like encephalopathies?
d27.rationale: While central hyperventilation is a hallmark of RNU2-2 DEE, episodic hyperventilation also occurs in Rett syndrome (MECP2), FOXG1 syndrome, and Pitt-Hopkins syndrome (TCF4). Determining comparative likelihood ratios will delineate its specificity among syndromic respiratory dysrhythmias.

d28.question_text: Does hyperventilation occur in biallelic/recessive RNU2-2 neurodevelopmental disorders at comparable rates to the dominant de novo n.4G>A and n.35A>G cohorts?
d28.rationale: Jackson et al. and Leitao et al. identified biallelic RNU2-2 cases as mechanistically distinct with reduced U2-2 stability. Comparing HPO terms across biallelic versus dominant cohorts will determine whether respiratory rhythm dysregulation is specific to dominant-negative spliceosomal alleles.

d29.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Recessive biallelic RNU2-2 variants exhibit a significantly earlier median age of seizure onset (infancy, median 10.5 to 18 months) and higher rates of epileptic spasms / tonic seizures compared to dominant de novo RNU2-2 variants.
d29.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Henry et al. (2026) report an infantile median onset age of 10.5 months in biallelic cases with predominant infantile spasms/tonic seizures and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome-like presentation, whereas Leitão et al. (2026) report a higher median onset of 1.5 years (18 months) with onset extending up to 16 years.; Jackson et al. (2026) state that the recessive RNU2-2 condition is clinically and mechanistically distinct from the dominant disorder, whereas Leitão et al. (2026) conclude that dominant and recessive forms share extensive phenotypic overlap and represent a biological gradient of impact across noncoding snRNA variants.

d30.question_text: Does direct head-to-head comparison of standardized semiology (epileptic spasms, tonic seizures, myoclonic seizures) between age-matched dominant and recessive RNU2-2 cohorts demonstrate statistically significant separation?
d30.rationale: Current cohorts differ in ascertainment (epilepsy genetics clinics versus general rare disease cohorts), confounding apparent differences in seizure onset age and predominant semiologies.

d31.question_text: Do specific 5' snRNA domain variant configurations dictate early-infantile spasm presentation versus later childhood DEE within biallelic RNU2-2 patients?
d31.rationale: Biallelic cases exhibit broad variation in onset (8 weeks to 16 years); determining whether structural disruption of U2-2 snRNA core base-pairing correlates with infantile spasm onset would explain cohort discordance.

d32.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: The diagnostic yield of dominant de novo RNU2-2 pathogenic variants in unselected or previously unsolved DEE cohorts is between 0.5% and 2.0% (approximately 3 to 10 cases per 500-1000 DEE patients).
d32.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: The hypothesis attributes the 0.5%-2.0% diagnostic yield in unsolved DEE cohorts specifically to dominant de novo RNU2-2 variants, whereas recent systematic sequencing studies show that severe RNU2-2 DEE can also be driven by ultra-rare biallelic (recessive) variants clustering in 5' domains.; Cohort re-analysis yields vary depending on whether the cohort selection is limited to complex drug-resistant pediatric epilepsies, specific DEE subtypes (e.g., infantile epileptic spasms syndrome/Lennox-Gastaut syndrome phenotypes), or broad unselected neurodevelopmental disorder cohorts.

d33.question_text: What is the relative breakdown of dominant de novo versus biallelic recessive pathogenic variants in RNU2-2 across large prospective unselected DEE cohorts (>1000 patients)?
d33.rationale: Clarifying the inheritance modes will determine whether dominant de novo or recessive loss-of-function variants predominate in DEE cohorts and settle the exact yield attributable to each mechanism.

d34.question_text: Can RNA-sequencing on patient-derived fibroblasts or peripheral blood reliably distinguish dominant RNU2-2 mis-splicing profiles from biallelic U2-2 abundance decreases?
d34.rationale: Henry et al. demonstrated distinct splicing changes in fibroblasts for biallelic variants, while Jackson et al. observed transcript destabilization and altered U2-2/U2-1 ratios. A direct functional biomarker assay would resolve ambiguous VUS findings.

d35.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: The divergent epilepsy penetrance and severity between dominant and recessive RNU2-2 disorders are driven by distinct molecular mechanisms: dominant mutations act via a dominant-negative, toxic spliceosomal disruption, whereas recessive mutations cause quantitative loss of U2-2 snRNA transcript abundance.
d35.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Jackson et al. (2026) report that recessive RNU2-2 syndrome is mechanistically distinct from dominant disorder due to reduced transcript stability/abundance, whereas Henry et al. (2026) demonstrate that biallelic variants directly lead to spliceosomal dysfunction with missplicing (alternate 3' splice sites and mutually exclusive exons) in patient fibroblasts.; Leitão et al. (2026) propose a gradient-of-impact model linking dominant and recessive variants with overlapping phenotypes and variant-specific splicing and episignature impacts, contradicting a clean binary dichotomy of dominant-negative toxicity versus purely quantitative transcript loss.

d36.question_text: Does tissue-specific expression of RNU2-2 and its paralog RNU2-1 modulate spliceosomal misprocessing in neural versus non-neural cell types?
d36.rationale: Blood transcriptomics failed to detect the missplicing readily evident in fibroblasts in Henry et al. (2026); resolving tissue-specific U2-2:U2-1 stoichiometry in neuronal lineages will clarify whether quantitative depletion leads directly to downstream spliceosomal errors.

d37.question_text: Do dominant and recessive RNU2-2 variants induce convergent or distinct genome-wide DNA episignatures?
d37.rationale: Leitão et al. noted variant-specific episignatures; comparing episignature patterns across large cohorts of dominant vs biallelic cases can objectively quantify whether epigenetic dysregulation reflects a shared gradient or mutually exclusive mechanistic pathways.

d38.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Epilepsy penetrance in dominant de novo RNU2-2 cases is virtually complete (>95%) while in biallelic recessive cases penetrance is incomplete (~80-85%), leaving a subset of recessive patients who present with intellectual disability without clinical seizures.
d38.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Greene et al. report in their abstract that all 25 dominant cases displayed a severe seizure phenotype, but also note in the text that 'Seizure' was coded/annotated in 89% of cases, conflicting with the claim of >95% penetrance.; Schatz et al. (2026) report variable expressivity and individuals presenting with 'no seizure phenotype' in RNU2-2 disorders, contradicting complete or near-complete penetrance.

d39.question_text: What proportion of dominant versus recessive RNU2-2 patients remain seizure-free into late adolescence and adulthood in unselected neurodevelopmental cohorts?
d39.rationale: Ascertainment bias from cohorts recruited specifically for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) may artificially elevate reported epilepsy penetrance compared to broad intellectual disability cohorts.

d40.question_text: Do specific secondary alleles or modifying variants (such as n.99A) account for reduced seizure penetrance in non-epileptic carriers of pathogenic RNU2-2 alleles?
d40.rationale: Leitão et al. highlighted specific variants modifying penetrance; determining molecular modifiers could explain why a subset of patients with pathogenic variants escape clinical epilepsy.

d41.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for brain MRI findings (such as hippocampal sclerosis or delayed myelination) across dominant versus recessive RNU2-2 cohorts?
d41.rationale: Chiu et al. (2026) identified hippocampal sclerosis in 3 of 5 dominant patients; comparing this directly to Leitao et al.'s 35 dominant and 91 recessive patients will establish if structural hippocampal changes are a specific imaging biomarker.

d42.question_text: Does the frequency of autonomic/respiratory dysregulation (hyperventilation vs central sleep apnea) differ between RNU2-2 position 4 and position 35 dominant variant carriers?
d42.rationale: Greene et al. established that dominant RNU2-2 variants recur specifically at positions 4 and 35. Comparing clinical tables between these two positional hotspots will clarify genotype-phenotype correlations within dominant DEE119.

d43.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence and semiology of movement disorders (e.g. choreoathetosis, dystonia, tremor) across the 35 dominant and 91 recessive RNU2-2 cases reported by Leitão et al. compared directly to RNU4-2 cohorts?
d43.rationale: Krygier et al. and Henry et al. point to hyperkinesia as a hallmark, but systematic counts per cohort across the Leitão et al. 141 individuals are required to establish true diagnostic sensitivity and specificity.

d44.question_text: Does sleep-activated epileptiform discharge or electrical status epilepticus in sleep (ESES/CSWS) correlate specifically with hippocampal sclerosis and respiratory dysrhythmias in dominant RNU2-2 DEE?
d44.rationale: Chiu et al. documented sleep-activated epileptiform discharges in 4/5 and status epilepticus in 5/5, suggesting a distinct sleep-epilepsy-autonomic circuit vulnerability in RNU2-2 not shared with other spliceosomopathies.

d45.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): In the dominant DEE119 subcohort of Leitao et al. (2026), status epilepticus (HP:0002133) and focal/bilateral tonic-clonic seizures exceed 70% prevalence (>=25/35), whereas infantile epileptic spasms (HP:0012469) are present in fewer than 20% (<7/35), distinguishing dominant DEE119 from early-infancy recessive RNU2-2 encephalopathy.
d45.rationale: deep test refuted it: The specific quantitative claim that status epilepticus (HP:0002133) and focal/bilateral tonic-clonic seizures exceed 70% prevalence (>=25/35) while infantile epileptic spasms are present in <20% (<7/35) in the Leitão et al. dominant cohort is not supported by the available source text. Moreover, the proposed distinction between dominant DEE119 and recessive RNU2-2 encephalopathy based on status epilepticus fails because status epilepticus is also highly prevalent in biallelic recessive RNU2-2 DEE (57%, 8/14 patients in Henry et al. 2026), and Leitão et al. explicitly note that dominant and recessive RNU2-2 forms share overlapping clinical features.

d46.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for specific seizure semiologies (infantile spasms vs. focal/bilateral tonic-clonic seizures vs. status epilepticus) across the full 35 dominant RNU2-2 patients in Leitão et al.?
d46.rationale: A comprehensive table extracted from the full clinical supplement of Leitão et al. is required to establish whether seizure semiology statistically differs between dominant and recessive RNU2-2 cohorts.

d47.question_text: Does median age of seizure onset (e.g. 24 months in dominant vs. early infancy in recessive) provide better phenotypic discrimination than status epilepticus occurrence?
d47.rationale: Chiu et al. reported an onset age around 24 months in dominant cases, whereas recessive cohorts manifest with early-infancy spasms, suggesting onset timing rather than status epilepticus alone may be the discriminating feature.

d48.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Episodic hyperventilation is a selective phenotypic discriminator of dominant de novo RNU2-2 DEE, occurring in >50% of dominant cases but <10% of recessive biallelic RNU2-2 cases and <2% of RNU4-2 cases.
d48.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Small initial cohorts (Chiu et al., Krygier et al.) report hyperventilation in a majority (3/5) of dominant de novo RNU2-2 patients, leading to diagnostic classification entries denoting seizures and hyperventilation; however, larger cohorts (Leitão et al.) observe substantial clinical overlap across 35 dominant and 91 recessive individuals along an allelic gradient.; Quantitative claims of hyperventilation prevalence below 10% in recessive RNU2-2 and below 2% in RNU4-2 lack direct cohort-wide comparative frequency data across standardized diagnostic registries.

d49.question_text: What is the systematic HPO-coded prevalence of episodic hyperventilation (HP:0002883) across the complete international cohort of 35 dominant versus 91 biallelic RNU2-2 patients described by Leitão et al.?
d49.rationale: Resolving this question with exact numerators and denominators will determine whether episodic hyperventilation maintains statistical power as an independent clinical discriminator between dominant and recessive forms.

d50.question_text: Does episodic hyperventilation in RNU2-2 DEE represent central autonomic dysregulation or an ictal/peri-ictal epileptic phenomenon (e.g., autonomic seizure component or post-ictal hyperpnea)?
d50.rationale: Krygier et al. noted hyperventilation episodes immediately preceding generalized tonic-clonic seizures, whereas Chiu et al. and OMIM report it alongside obstructive sleep apnea. Video-EEG polysomnography correlation is required to establish its pathophysiological basis.

d51.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: The combination of hippocampal sclerosis on brain MRI and sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges is present in >50% of dominant RNU2-2 DEE individuals, distinguishing them from RNU4-2 ReNU syndrome where structural hippocampal sclerosis is virtually absent.
d51.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Small initial case series (Chiu et al., n=5) reported hippocampal sclerosis in 3/5 (60%) and sleep-activated multifocal discharges in 4/5 (80%), whereas larger multi-center dominant cohorts (Greene et al., n=25; Leit�ao et al., n=35) highlight severe refractory seizures, hyperventilation, hypotonia, and microcephaly without establishing hippocampal sclerosis in >50% of dominant individuals.; It remains unproven whether hippocampal sclerosis is an intrinsic primary neurodevelopmental feature of dominant RNU2-2 or an acquired secondary sequela of prolonged status epilepticus and recurrent febrile/hemiclonic seizures occurring in early childhood.
